title: Chelsea’s unaccountable executives have built a monument to hubris
content:
On the ninth of Liam Rosenior’s 107 days in charge of Chelsea, his goalkeeper Robert Sanchez made two horrible mistakes that led to goals during the Carabao Cup semi-final first leg against Arsenal.

Those errors were the first thing he was asked about his post-match press conference. Rosenior nodded earnestly in recognition of the question, his eyes narrowing, before replying that he didn’t blame Sanchez at all. “I said to Rob before the game — and I made this really clear — when my players make mistakes, I’m accountable,” the coach said. “That’s on me.”

It’s the kind of messaging that is popular among younger coaches, eager to promote a warm, trusting environment, far removed from the authoritarian regimes of the past.

But did Rosenior realise what he was saying? At Chelsea, of all clubs, no one needs to be told the buck stops with the coach. Their players, many of them on extraordinarily long contracts, have clearly felt secure enough to make mistakes without fearing the consequences. The only people less accountable are the owners, executives and recruitment specialists whose much-trumpeted Chelsea project has become a monument to hubris.

How Rosenior’s muddled tactics left Chelsea a bedraggled mess

Rosenior never commanded authority at Chelsea. He was doomed from the start

Why Champions League football is essential to BlueCo’s model

Four key reasons Rosenior’s position became untenable

Chelsea’s unaccountable executives have built a monument to hubris

Over the past four years, criticism of this Chelsea ownership and executive regime — whether by fans or by the media — has often met with smug or defiant responses. Wednesday evening’s statement, explaining the decision to part company with Rosenior, carried a distinctly more humble tone. As well as the public statement mentioning the need for a “process of self-reflection”, there was a recognition from the club hierarchy more privately that “we do not always get every decision right” and an emphasis on “a real focus on learning from this moment”.

One would hope so. For all the criticism and derision heaped on him, much of it vindictive, this is not on Rosenior. The various mistakes he made, whether tactical or interpersonal, reflect far less on him than on the decision-makers who felt the answer to another crisis in January, following the abrupt, acrimonious departure of Enzo Maresca in January, was to parachute in another inexperienced coach whose days appeared numbered even as the ink was drying on his six-and-a-half-year contract.

It will be four years next month since BlueCo, an investment consortium led by Todd Boehly and Clearlake Capital, completed their £2.35billion ($2.97bn) acquisition of Chelsea.

In that time Boehly, Behdad Eghbali and their team of sporting directors, led by Laurence Stewart and Paul Winstanley, have taken a wrecking ball to the football industry’s conventional thinking, spending dizzying sums on dizzying numbers of players, handing out seven, eight and nine-year contracts to numerous youngsters in the same positions, telling themselves and the world that this is what future-proofing looks like and doing it all with the unmistakable and seemingly unshakable certainty of the disruptor.

Under BlueCo’s ownership, Chelsea have committed approximately £1.5billion ($2bn) on player transfer fees. It is, in an era of wild excess among Europe’s richest clubs, almost double what any rival has spent over the same period — and whereas Paris Saint-Germain’s £839m outlay has turned an underachieving squad into arguably the best in Europe, with Nuno Mendes, Vitinha, Joao Neves, Desire Doue and Khvicha Kvaratskhelia excelling under a world-class coach in Luis Enrique, even the most generous analysis would struggle to claim more than a handful of BlueCo’s signings have strengthened Chelsea in a meaningful way.

There is a point at which it is important to highlight that Chelsea have something tangible to show for the past four years.

Last season, under Maresca, they won the UEFA Conference League (for which they qualified by finishing sixth in the Premier League in 2023-24) and the FIFA Club World Cup (for which they qualified by winning the Champions League in 2021 under Roman Abramovich’s ownership). Their 3-0 victory over that brilliant PSG team in the Club World Cup final was one of those days — there were three or four of them over the course of last year — when it was possible to wonder whether, despite everything, the sheer volume of money spent on footballers brought a certain inevitability that Chelsea would find themselves on the right track after all.

But there is nothing inevitable about success when a club’s decision-makers appear so insistent that experience — on the field, in the dugout or even in the front office — is overrated.

How many times over the past four years have we heard Chelsea’s coaches — Graham Potter, Frank Lampard in his brief interim spell, Mauricio Pochettino, Maresca, even the hitherto upbeat Rosenior in his miserable final week— highlight weaknesses in this squad? All of those coaches started out with the same wide-eyed enthusiasm, talking about exciting players with potential. All of them, before long, were left lamenting a lack of battle-hardened experience and knowhow or, as Rosenior put it after the abject 3-0 defeat at Brighton & Hove Albion on Tuesday, a failure to do “the basics of football”.

Lampard, dismayed in the spring of 2023 by the lack of individual and collective responsibility among a group of players assembled at such expense, used the same expression, “the basics of football”. Pochettino, trying to explain a miserable 2-2 draw at home to Burnley in March 2024, pointed to his head and heart and said what his players lacked was “the capacity, the energy, the hunger, that is the minimum to compete in the Premier League”. Maresca said before, during and after last summer’s transfer window that it was important to add more experienced players, not just to improve an inconsistent team but to help the younger ones develop.

Every season ends with the coach calling for more proven players. Every summer transfer window brings another flurry of younger players. Among last summer’s intake, costing a shade under £300m, all of them signed between the ages of 18 and 23, the only regular starter in the Premier League has been centre-forward Joao Pedro. Brazilian teenager Estevao had been by far the best of the rest until his season was cut short by injury. Among the others — defenders Mamadou Sarr and Jorrel Hato, midfielder Dario Essugo, wingers Jamie Gittens and Alejandro Garnacho and centre-forward Liam Delap — some have shown glimpses of potential but little or nothing to improve a team whose need for proven performers was and still is obvious.

Of the 42 players Chelsea have signed since January 2023, at a total cost of more than £1billion ($1.35bn), more than half (23) were signed between the ages of 18 and 20. A further nine were 21 or 22. Of the remaining 10, who were recruited between the ages of 23 and 26, only Sanchez (signed at 25), Tosin Adarabioyo (signed at 26), Pedro Neto (signed at 24) and Joao Pedro (signed at 23) have been part of this season’s squad.

The theory has been that an approach built around youth allows players to mature and develop into leaders. But in a volatile environment, in a dressing room that is short of leaders and role models, under a succession of coaches who are not given the time to establish any authority, at a club where player trading appears to have taken precedence over team-building, there is little sign of that.

It is easy to imagine that in an elite environment, learning from a top-class coach and top-class players, Enzo Fernandez, an Argentinian World Cup winner signed for £106m ($143m) in January 2023, would have gone from strength to strength and become that type of leader rather than a symbol of Chelsea’s dissatisfaction. To put it in terms that might appeal to the club’s owners, a £106m asset might have matured into a £150m asset. But while Manchester City are considering signing him this summer, talk of Chelsea making a profit seems optimistic in the extreme; they overpaid for him three years ago and, in an inconsistent, incoherent team, his development has been fitful.

And Fernandez, along with Cole Palmer, Moises Caicedo, Joao Pedro and Estavao, has been among their better signings — in terms of impact, if not necessarily value for money. It comes to something when a club has spent £1.5billion in the transfer market over a four-year period and only two players, the much-criticised Sanchez and the unsettled Fernandez, have started more games in this season’s Premier League than homegrown defender Trevoh Chalobah, who in the summer of 2024 was forced to train away from the first team, stripped of his squad number and sent on loan to Crystal Palace before being recalled and reintegrated barely four months later.

So many other players have come and gone without making the slightest impression. Some are cited as successes (Djordje Petrovic, Noni Madueke, Renato Veiga, Lesley Ugochukwu) because the club has managed to sell them on for a profit. All leading clubs consider resale value when signing players, but at Chelsea the club’s entire football operation appears to have been built around that principle rather than, as the coaches see it, what the team needs. Supporters, meanwhile, are just more interested in results.

The real test of Chelsea’s business might be looming. Failure to qualify for the Champions League — or even the Europa League or Conference League — would severely impact revenue at a club where matchday income is constrained by the limitations of Stamford Bridge and whose commercial growth has stalled. As explained in depth here, there will be pressure to raise funds this summer and the obvious way to do so is by selling players. The challenge will be to generate enough money by selling unwanted players — of which there are many — so that they do not have to sell those, such as Caicedo and Palmer, whom they would ideally build around.

It bears repeating that Chelsea are eighth in the Premier League table, closer to the relegation zone than the top. And rather than some alarming low point for this regime, it is familiar territory. They finished 12th in season one with just 44 points, winning 11 of their 38 games. They finished sixth in season two with 63 points (18 wins) but even most of that campaign was spent grubbing around in mid-table. Season three, under Maresca, was better (fourth place with 69 points and 20 wins) but they were still, after a dramatic late run, only four points above seventh-placed Nottingham Forest. And while the Rosenior appointment clearly backfired, they were already 15 points off the pace in the Premier League, with just eight wins from their first 19 games, when they parted with Maresca on January 1.

There have certainly been moments over the past 12 months in which Chelsea have looked like a credible team: the final weeks of last term, the Conference League and Club World Cup successes, impressive early-season victories over Liverpool and Barcelona, even the wins at Aston Villa and Napoli under Rosenior. But these were sporadic high points. In a season and a half under Maresca, they won just 26 out of 57 Premier League matches. That his average of 1.74 points per game represents the high watermark of the BlueCo era (as opposed to 1.27 points per game under Potter, 1.66 under Pochettino and 1.31 under Rosenior) seems less an endorsement of Maresca and more an indictment of the entire period.

They will always have East Rutherford, of course: that surreal day at MetLife Stadium last July when they outclassed PSG in the Club World Cup final and shared the victory podium with President Donald Trump. But nine months on, that particular crown looks almost as ill-fitting as Trump’s FIFA Peace Prize.

It will be Chelsea’s title for another three years until the next edition of the tournament. It is quite possible that, by 2029, a team containing Reece James, Levi Colwill, Caicedo, Palmer, Estevao and others will have grown into a genuine force in the Premier League. But who can say which of the long-term investments the club has made — and the long-term contracts — will have paid dividends by then, given this regime’s mediocre record to date?

So much will hinge on getting the next appointment right. Not passable, the way the Maresca and (to a lesser extent) Pochettino hires were passable, but right. If the Rosenior experiment has underlined anything, it is what was already apparent to all but the Chelsea hierarchy: that this is a club and a group of players that needs to be managed with a firm hand.

The names of Marco Silva and Andoni Iraola, out of contract at Fulham and Bournemouth, spring to mind. So too — fleetingly — does that of Unai Emery. But Emery, despite certain financial constraints, is onto a good thing at Aston Villa, on course for Champions League qualification again and through to the Europa League semi-finals. Even Silva and Iraola would be excused for giving this Chelsea a wide berth. As the club’s former captain John Terry said in a social media lament on Wednesday night, “Is a real top manager going to come to Chelsea Football Club at the moment with the position we’re in?”

It has just gone three years since, reflecting on their first season under BlueCo ownership, this column argued that Chelsea were in danger of becoming “unmanageable … where coaches come and go and nothing changes because the culture inside both the club and the dressing room is one of dysfunction”. And while there have been fluctuations since, what does it say about this regime that the same failings persist?

There has been so much upheaval in some areas — the head coach, the playing squad, even in other departments inside the Stamford Bridge offices — and yet faith in this long-term strategy, led by Stewart and Winstanley, overseen by Boehly and Eghbali, has appeared unshakeable.

Rosenior didn’t need to tell anyone that the coach will be the one who is held accountable for others’ mistakes as well as his own. At Chelsea, it has long been clear where the buck stops and where it doesn’t.
